name: Philippa of Hainault
title: Queen of England

summary: Daughter of the count of Hainaut and wife of Edward III for forty-one years: mother of the Black Prince and John of Gaunt, patron of Jean Froissart, and the queen remembered for pleading for the lives of the burghers of Calais.
overview: Philippa of Hainault married Edward III in 1328 as the price of the Hainuyer ships and troops that carried Queen Isabella's invasion. She became a popular queen and the mother of a large royal family, and her intercession for the burghers of Calais in 1347 became the most famous story of the Hundred Years' War.
greatestFeats: Mother of Edward the Black Prince, Lionel of Antwerp, John of Gaunt and Edmund of Langley
Interceded for the six burghers of Calais in 1347
Patron of the chronicler Jean Froissart
Gave her name to The Queen's College, Oxford

birth.note: Her birth date is uncertain; several years between 1310 and 1315 have been proposed.

death.circumstance: Died at Windsor after a long illness, with Edward III beside her.

quickFacts.knownFor: Pleading for the burghers of Calais and her patronage of Froissart

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Philippa of Hainault was queen of England from 1328 to 1369 as the wife of Edward III. Her marriage was the price of the ships and soldiers her father's county lent Queen Isabella for the invasion of 1326, but it became one of the most successful royal marriages of the fourteenth century, lasting forty-one years and producing a dozen or more children, among them Edward the Black Prince, Lionel of Antwerp, John of Gaunt and Edmund of Langley.

She was a popular queen, credited with encouraging Flemish weavers to settle in England, a patron of chroniclers and scholars, and the heroine of the best-known story of the Hundred Years' War: her plea to Edward to spare the six burghers of Calais in 1347.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Philippa was born around 1310–1315, probably at Valenciennes, one of the daughters of William the Good, Count of Hainaut, Holland and Zeeland, and Joan of Valois, a niece of Philip IV of France. In 1326 Queen Isabella, in exile with her son Edward, agreed his betrothal to one of the count's daughters in return for the troops and ships that carried her invasion to England. Philippa came to England in December 1327 and married Edward III at York Minster on 24 January 1328.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Froissart, who entered her service in 1361 and owed her his start as a writer, praised her generosity, piety and good sense, and his warm portrait has shaped her reputation ever since. The picture is flattering but not empty: her household accounts show large charitable gifts and even larger debts, and Edward III relied on her as a steadying presence at a court built on chivalric display.

Her famous intercession needs care. Jean le Bel, writing within a few years, tells how the pregnant queen knelt before Edward and begged him to spare the six burghers who had come out of Calais with ropes around their necks; it was a political ritual as much as an act of mercy, letting the king show clemency at his queen's request. Froissart's further claim that she rallied the English army before the victory over the Scots at Neville's Cross in 1346 finds no support in English sources.

contentSections.title: Queen of Edward III
paragraphs: Philippa was crowned at Westminster in February 1330, and in June she gave birth to her first son, Edward, at Woodstock. The birth of an heir strengthened the young king's position months before he overthrew Roger Mortimer. She travelled with Edward on campaign in the Low Countries in 1338–1340, giving birth to Lionel at Antwerp and John at Ghent, and in 1346–1347 she joined him at the siege of Calais.

Her Hainuyer connections shaped the court. Jean Froissart, from Valenciennes, served as her clerk and wrote her praises, and her compatriot Walter Manny became one of Edward's leading captains. In 1341 her chaplain Robert de Eglesfield founded The Queen's College at Oxford and named it in her honour.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Philippa fell ill in the later 1360s and died at Windsor Castle on 15 August 1369. Froissart, who was not present, wrote that on her deathbed she asked Edward to pay her debts, honour her gifts to the Church and be buried beside her at Westminster. Her tomb effigy, carved by the sculptor Jean de Liège, is one of the earliest realistic portraits in English royal sculpture, showing a stout, middle-aged woman rather than an idealised queen.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Philippa's sons founded the houses whose rivalries dominated the next century: the descendants of John of Gaunt became the House of Lancaster, and those of Edmund of Langley the House of York. Her patronage made Froissart the chronicler of the Hundred Years' War, and the Calais story became a favourite subject for later painters and for Rodin's Burghers of Calais.
